title: Predictively-Oriented Kalman Filtering
claim: Standard and generalised-Bayes filters become over-confident or mis-calibrated under misspecification; ours widens uncertainty appropriately and still tracks the truth.
layout: 2x3 grid of plots, methods as columns, misspecification type as rows
description: A 2x3 grid of time-series plots. Columns are methods: KF, WoLF-IMQ and KF-PrO (ours). Rows are misspecification types: Outlier on top and Systematic on the bottom. Each panel shows black circles for observations, a red line for the true latent state and a grey band for the posterior predictive. In the Outlier row, KF's band spikes at each outlier and then recovers. WoLF-IMQ's band barely reacts. KF-PrO's band widens sharply at the outliers and then narrows again. In the Systematic row the true state jumps upward partway through. KF and WoLF-IMQ keep narrow bands that lag far below the data after the jump. KF-PrO's band widens at the jump and recovers quickly to cover the data. The eye goes first to the red step and the grey bands.
caption: Illustration on the Gaussian location model. Data $(y_k)_{k=1}^n$ are shown as circles and the true latent state is in red; in the top row the data are corrupted by outliers, while in the bottom row the model is systematically misspecified. Posterior predictives are displayed for \mkf (left), a generalised Bayes method called \mWlfImq due to [ref] (centre) and our proposed \mPrOKF (right).
abstract: This paper presents a post-Bayesian approach to online filtering in nonlinear state-space models, capable of avoiding over-confident inferences in settings where either the dynamical model, the measurement model, or both, could be misspecified. This is addressed using predictively oriented (PrO) posteriors, an emerging paradigm in which learning (i.e., posterior concentration) occurs if and only if the overall model is well-specified, without strict adherence to Bayes' theorem. As the characterisation of PrO posteriors is challenging, our main technical contribution is a fast approximate linear-Gaussian update procedure, analogous to an (iterated) extended Kalman filter. The methodology, which we call EKF-PrO, has no tunable hyper-parameters and has a computational cost comparable to that of existing filtering methods. Performance is empirically assessed on a range of linear and non-linear applications, in which the state-space model is systematically misspecified.
